title: Wider economic picture stalls BOQ
full_text:
Macroeconomic clouds loom over Bank of Queensland’s plans to return to growth in home lending this year.
The bank reported cash earnings after tax of $325m for the 12 months ended August 31, down 15 per cent on FY25, reflecting the previously disclosed $33m after-tax technology impairment charge, and higher loan impairment expenses of $54m.
Excluding notable items, cash earnings came in at $358m, still down 7 per cent on the prior corresponding period.
During the year BOQ completed its complex ME Bank migration and a $3.7bn asset sale to Challenger.
The bank’s statutory profit was $250m, an increase of 88 per cent, primarily due to FY25’s goodwill impairment.
Home lending growth fell 8 per cent to $4.63bn, while commercial loans jumped 16 per cent to $2.06bn.
Net interest margin was 1.70 per cent, up 6 basis points.
The regional lender told investors it remains committed to becoming “a simple, specialist bank”, as it completed its ME brand migration, transitioned mortgage origination to digital channels and continued to grow its business bank.
“FY26 was a year of consistent delivery for BOQ,” chief executive Rod Finch said.
“As we enter FY27, we are well positioned for a sustainable return to growth. While economic conditions remain uncertain, the foundations we have built give us confidence in our ability to deliver for our customers and shareholders.” A final dividend of 20c per share will be paid on November 19, adding to the first-half payout of 20c.
On the outlook, the bank echoed broader market concerns that consumer and business confidence continues to be weighed down by inflation, rising cash rates and geopolitical uncertainty.
“Further increases in the cash rate are possible and a reduction is not expected before calendar year 2028,” the bank said.
But it’s hoping a focus on digital mortgage expansion to additional channels and customer segments will deliver a “sustainable return to growth in home lending in FY27”. Commercial lending growth in FY27 is expected to be comparable to FY26.
UBS equity analyst John Storey said the FY26 outcome “reinforces the turnaround thesis but provides limited fresh impetus for earnings upgrades”. “Simplification, strategic execution and balance-sheet de-risking have supported the re-rating over the past year,” he said.
